params.title: Other GMDSS Equipment
params.subtitle: EPIRB, SART, survival craft VHF and NAVTEX: what they do, the numbers the exam asks about, and when parts must be replaced.

onScreen: EPIRB, SART, survival craft VHF and NAVTEX
scenes.narration: This lesson covers four pieces of GMDSS safety equipment you will maintain: the EPIRB, the SART, the survival craft VHF transceiver, and the NAVTEX receiver. For each one, we'll look at what it does, the numbers the exam asks about, and when its parts must be replaced. Let's start with the EPIRB, the Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon.

callouts.label: 5-watt 406 MHz alert beacon, transmitting on 406.025 MHz
121.5 MHz low-power homing transmitter, not the alert
Bracket magnet holds the switch safe: no accidental operation
No aural locator signal: found by radio homing and the strobe

scenes.narration: A 406 megahertz satellite EPIRB normally has three main parts: a 5-watt alert beacon on 406 megahertz, an automatic hydrostatic release, and a strobe light. The alert goes out on 406.025 megahertz. A separate 121.5 megahertz transmitter is only a low-power homing signal for searchers, not the alerting transmitter. The magnet in the mounting bracket holds the beacon's switch in the safe state, so it can't operate accidentally while it sits in the bracket. And there is no aural, or audible, locator signal: rescuers find the EPIRB by radio homing and by its flashing strobe light.

blocks.label: Shore database
blocks.note: EPIRB ID gives the vessel information

onScreen: Local User Terminal: Doppler shift gives position
Shore database: EPIRB ID gives vessel information
scenes.narration: When the EPIRB transmits, a COSPAS-SARSAT satellite picks up the alert, time-tags it, and relays it to any Local User Terminal, or LUT, in the satellite's view. The satellites are one-way relays: they do not provide follow-on search and rescue communications after the EPIRB is located. Rescuers use other radio and satellite links for that. At the Local User Terminal, the Doppler shift of the EPIRB signal is measured to calculate its position. The message also carries the EPIRB's ID number, which is used to look up the vessel's information in the shore database.

badges.label: EPIRB battery
badges.note: It must still give a full 48 hours of transmission

badges.label: Automatic release mechanism
badges.note: So it is sure to work if the ship sinks

onScreen: EPIRB battery: 5 years or after use
scenes.narration: Two replacement intervals to remember. The EPIRB battery must be replaced every 5 years, or after use, because any use drains capacity it needs for a full 48 hours of transmission. The automatic release mechanism, the hydrostatic release, must be replaced every 2 years, so it is sure to work if the ship sinks.

params.title: SART: Search And Rescue Radar Transponder
items: Operates in the 9 GHz band: answers 3 cm X-band radars at about 9.2–9.5 GHz
Does not answer 3 GHz S-band radars; 406 MHz is the EPIRB frequency
After activation it waits in standby and responds only to radar interrogation
Battery: replace every 5 years or after use; it must give 96 hours of standby, then 8 hours of transmission

onScreen: Not S-band; 406 MHz is the EPIRB
Standby until a radar interrogates it
scenes.narration: The SART, or Search And Rescue Radar Transponder, works with ships' radars. It operates in the 9 gigahertz band, answering 3 centimeter X-band radars at about 9.2 to 9.5 gigahertz. It does not answer 3 gigahertz S-band radars, and 406 megahertz belongs to the EPIRB, not the SART. Once activated, a SART waits in standby and responds only when a radar interrogates it; it does not start radiating the moment it is switched on. Its battery must be replaced every 5 years or after being used, because it must still provide 96 hours of standby followed by 8 hours of transmission.

params.title: A SART on the radar display
labels: Other ships and land show as ordinary echoes
The SART paints 12 equally spaced dots, outward from its position along its bearing
Very close in, the dots become arcs and then circles

onScreen: SART: 12 equally spaced dots outward along its bearing
scenes.narration: Here's what the SART looks like on the searching ship's radar. Other ships and land show as ordinary echoes. When the radar's beam reaches the SART, it answers, and its signal appears as a line of 12 equally spaced dots, extending outward from the SART's position along its bearing. They are dots, not dashes or spirals. As the searching ship closes in, very near the SART the dots become arcs and then complete circles.

params.title: Why 12 dots: the SART sweep
labels: Sweep of 0.4 µs across the entire 3 cm radar band
Returning sweep of 7.5 µs back to the beginning
Each 7.5 µs sweep crosses the radar's frequency once: one dot

scenes.narration: When it is interrogated, the SART starts with a sweep of 0.4 microseconds across the entire 3 centimeter radar band, followed by a returning sweep of 7.5 microseconds back to the beginning, for a total of 12 sweeps. The amber line is the searching radar's frequency. Each slow 7.5 microsecond sweep passes through that frequency once, and each pass paints one of the 12 dots.

params.title: Spacing between the dots
params.formula: d = one sweep cycle ÷ radar mile
params.answer: d ≈ 0.64 nm, at 5 miles or any other range

onScreen: d = one sweep cycle ÷ radar mile
scenes.narration: How far apart are the dots? Divide one complete sweep cycle by the radar mile. One cycle is 7.5 plus 0.4, or 7.9 microseconds. Divide by 12.34 microseconds per nautical mile, and you get about 0.64 nautical miles. The spacing is the same at any range, so a SART at a distance of 5 miles shows dots approximately 0.64 nautical miles apart.

callouts.label: Antenna permanently affixed: fixed and non-removable
Channel 16 (156.8 MHz) plus at least one other channel
Watertight to a depth of 1 meter for 5 minutes
Effective radiated power at least 0.25 watt
Battery: every 5 years or after use for distress communications

scenes.narration: Every survival craft carries a portable two-way VHF radio. Its antenna is fixed and non-removable, permanently affixed. Under GMDSS it must operate on channel 16, 156.8 megahertz, the voice distress and calling channel, plus at least one other channel. It must be watertight to a depth of 1 meter for 5 minutes. The minimum effective radiated power is 0.25 watt, not 1 watt: enough for short-range, on-scene communication, and easy on the battery. The minimum receiver sensitivity is 2.0 microvolts. And the battery must be changed every 5 years, or after use for distress communications, because it must still deliver 8 hours of operation when it is needed.

Here's how those frequencies line up. Channel 16, 156.8 megahertz, is the one the survival craft VHF must have. Channel 70 sits right beside it, but channel 70 is used only for digital selective calling, not simplex voice, so operating simplex on channel 70 is not a survival craft requirement. 121.5 megahertz is aeronautical, and 457.525 megahertz is an on-board UHF frequency. Neither is required.

onScreen: EPIRB, SART and survival craft VHF batteries: 5 years or after use
scenes.narration: Let's collect the intervals. The batteries in the EPIRB, the SART and the survival craft VHF are all replaced every 5 years, or after they have been used. The one to keep separate is the EPIRB's automatic release mechanism, which is replaced every 2 years.

onScreen: 2187.5 kHz: MF DSC distress, not NAVTEX
scenes.narration: Now NAVTEX, the automated broadcast of maritime safety information. 518 kilohertz is the primary frequency, used exclusively for NAVTEX broadcasts internationally, in English. 490 kilohertz carries national or local-language NAVTEX, and 4209.5 kilohertz is the HF NAVTEX frequency. Don't confuse these with 2187.5 kilohertz: that's an MF digital selective calling distress channel, not NAVTEX.

params.title: Programming a NAVTEX receiver
items: Broadcasts go out in categories of messages, each indicated by a single letter, in each station's scheduled time slots
Each transmitting station is identified by a single letter, not a two-digit number or a SELCALL
To reject messages, choose the category's single letter (A–Z) and deselect it
The receiver can be set to reject certain stations and message categories
Navigational warnings, meteorological warnings and search and rescue information cannot be turned off

onScreen: Reject a category: choose its letter, deselect it
Navigational, meteorological and SAR messages can't be turned off
scenes.narration: NAVTEX broadcasts are sent in categories of messages, each indicated by a single letter, and each station transmits in its own scheduled time slots rather than on request. Stations are identified by a single letter too, not a two-digit number or a SELCALL. You can program the receiver to reject certain stations and message categories: choose the category's single-letter identifier, A to Z, and deselect it. But three kinds of messages can never be turned off: navigational warnings, meteorological warnings, and search and rescue information.

params.title: How NAVTEX keeps messages accurate
labels: Each character is sent twice, with a time interval between the copies
Collective FEC: the repeat follows about 280 ms later
The receiver prints whichever copy arrives correctly

scenes.narration: Accuracy is ensured by sending each character twice, with a time interval between the two copies. This is called collective forward error correction, or FEC, and the repeat follows about 280 milliseconds later. If a burst of noise wipes out one copy, as it does here, the receiver simply uses the copy that arrived correctly, so the printed message is still clean.

callouts.label: Powers on and works normally; station settings are correct
But no new messages arrive for an extended period
Most likely cause: a defective RF amplifier at the antenna base
The amplifier is powered through the coax

onScreen: No new messages for a long time
Defective RF amplifier at the antenna base
scenes.narration: A common fault: the NAVTEX receiver powers on and appears to be working normally, and the station settings are correct, yet no new messages have arrived for an extended period. The most likely source of the problem is a defective RF amplifier at the base of the antenna. That amplifier is powered through the coax from the receiver.
